caption:
Apple's new annual report adds AI agents to its list of business risks.
The filing says agents may act in "unintended or unpredictable ways," including moves nobody directed or authorized.
Apple also admits its control over other companies' agents may be limited, even as it pushes to make Siri do more.

Would you let an AI agent spend money from your phone?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: TRT World, AI Weekly · Photos: Reuters, AppleInsider, 9to5Mac, The Apple Post

paragraphs.text: Apple has added autonomous AI agents to the list of risks in its annual report. The 10-K for fiscal 2026, filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on November 3, 2026, says agents may behave in unintended or unpredictable ways, including by taking actions that were not directed, instructed or authorized, according to reports by TRT World, Briefs Finance and AI Weekly.
The filing arrived one day after Apple reported its fourth quarter results and CEO John Ternus spoke with analysts on the earnings call, TRT World reported.
What the filing says agents can do

Apple describes agents that can run or modify software code, send messages and complete transactions on their own. The company says these systems may reach internal or external systems without the permissions they need, and that they could bypass security and control measures or be exploited by malicious actors, according to TRT World and JKN.

The report also warns that such technologies may conceal actions, withhold or manipulate information, or generate inaccurate or deceptive outputs, AI Weekly reported. Apple adds that some consequences, such as deleted data or completed transactions, may be difficult or impossible to reverse. JKN noted that small errors in multistep workflows could compound into outcomes that are hard to undo.

Apple says the risk is not limited to its own software. Its ability to oversee and control third party AI agents and other technologies may be limited, according to the filing as quoted by Briefs Finance and AI Weekly. The company also lists lawsuits, reputational harm, higher compliance costs from changing AI laws and public concern about autonomous systems as possible business risks.

The filing also says the legal and regulatory environment around AI and superintelligence remains uncertain, and that the use of AI in building operating systems, apps and services may add risks from errors, bugs or vulnerabilities, TRT World and JKN reported.

The warning comes as Apple widens what Siri can do. Briefs Finance reported that the current Siri AI, rolled out this fall, pulls information such as calendar entries and email from on device storage but does not run autonomously for long stretches. On the earnings call, Ternus said there is real room to expand Siri's capabilities and stressed that users should know what data and systems they are giving agents access to.

Apple also changed how Full Disk Access works on Macs in October to reduce the risk of granting that permission to AI agents, according to Briefs Finance and TRT World. Its developer guidance tells app makers to limit agent permissions and to treat untrusted content as data rather than commands, with indirect prompt injection named as a major threat, JKN reported.

The disclosure lands as rivals ship agent products. Briefs Finance noted that OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse can run tasks such as sending emails on their own, and that companies including Amazon and JPMorgan Chase are writing policies for agent access to their services.

Risk factor sections are written by lawyers to cover many outcomes, so the language does not mean Apple expects a specific failure. Still, the detail is notable. Apple is describing the exact behaviors that make agents useful, such as sending messages and paying for things, as the same behaviors that could expose it to lawsuits. That framing suggests Apple will keep tight permission controls on Siri and on third party agents running on its devices.

The next signal is how far Apple lets Siri act across third party apps without step by step confirmation, and whether its permission rules for outside agents get stricter on iPhone as they did for Full Disk Access on the Mac.
